```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 15.5

#| dev: ragg_png

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 1. CLEAN DATA
# --------------------------------------------------

df_plot <- ws %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(wearables),
    wearables != "",
    !str_detect(wearables, "ImportId"),
    !str_detect(wearables, "Wearables and biosignals")
  ) %>%
  mutate(

    # Background
    background = case_when(
      str_detect(position, "Psychology") ~ "🧠 Psychology /\nCog Neuro",
      str_detect(position, "Computer|Engineering|Data") ~ "💻 Engineering /\nCS / Data",
      str_detect(position, "Other|Multidisciplinary") ~ "🔀 Multidisciplinary /\nother",
      TRUE ~ "🔀 Multidisciplinary /\nother"
    ),
    background = factor(
      background,
      levels = c(
        "🧠 Psychology /\nCog Neuro",
        "💻 Engineering /\nCS / Data",
        "🔀 Multidisciplinary /\nother"
      )
    ),

    # Wearable experience
    wearable_exp = case_when(
      str_detect(wearables, "Curious Spectator") ~ "🕵️ Curious\nspectator",
      str_detect(wearables, "Casual User") ~ "⌚ Casual user /\nenthusiast",
      str_detect(wearables, "Hands-on Explorer") ~ "🧪 Hands-on\nexplorer",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    wearable_exp = factor(
      wearable_exp,
      levels = c(
        "🕵️ Curious\nspectator",
        "⌚ Casual user /\nenthusiast",
        "🧪 Hands-on\nexplorer"
      )
    ),

    # Current wearable use
    wearable_now = case_when(
      str_detect(warables.worn, "^No") ~ "No",
      str_detect(warables.worn, "^Yes") &
        !is.na(warables.worn_1_TEXT) &
        warables.worn_1_TEXT != "" ~ warables.worn_1_TEXT,
      str_detect(warables.worn, "^Yes") ~ "Yes, unspecified",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),

    # Psychophysiology / biosignals background
    biosignal_exp = case_when(
      str_detect(biosignals, "Psycho-what") ~ "🤷 Psycho-what?",
      str_detect(biosignals, "Textbook Level") ~ "📚 Textbook\nlevel",
      str_detect(biosignals, "Applied / UX Interest") ~ "🥼 Applied /\nUX interest",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    biosignal_exp = factor(
      biosignal_exp,
      levels = c(
        "🤷 Psycho-what?",
        "📚 Textbook\nlevel",
        "🥼 Applied /\nUX interest"
      )
    ),

    # Relationship with data analysis
    data_exp = case_when(
      str_detect(data.analysis, "complicated|Complicated") ~ "💔 It's\ncomplicated",
      str_detect(data.analysis, "Good friends") ~ "🤝 Good\nfriends",
      str_detect(data.analysis, "serious relationship") ~ "🔥 Serious\nrelationship",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    data_exp = factor(
      data_exp,
      levels = c(
        "💔 It's\ncomplicated",
        "🤝 Good\nfriends",
        "🔥 Serious\nrelationship"
      )
    ),

    # R experience
    r_exp_short = case_when(
      str_detect(R_exp, "R... who") ~ "🟩 R... who?",
      str_detect(R_exp, "Copy-Paste Warrior") ~ "🟨 Copy-paste\nwarrior",
      str_detect(R_exp, "Comfortable-ish") ~ "🟧 Comfortable-\nish",
      str_detect(R_exp, "Wizard") ~ "🟪 R wizard",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    r_exp_short = factor(
      r_exp_short,
      levels = c(
        "🟩 R... who?",
        "🟨 Copy-paste\nwarrior",
        "🟧 Comfortable-\nish",
        "🟪 R wizard"
      )
    ),

    # Expected attendance
    attendance = case_when(
      str_detect(attending, "Yes, count me in") ~ "All sessions",
      str_detect(attending, "Mostly yes") ~ "Most sessions",
      str_detect(attending, "Unsure") ~ "Unsure",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    attendance = factor(
      attendance,
      levels = c(
        "All sessions",
        "Most sessions",
        "Unsure"
      )
    )
  )

# --------------------------------------------------
# 2. OTHER SOFTWARE

software_df <- df_plot %>%
  separate_rows(other_software, sep = ",") %>%
  mutate(
    software = str_trim(other_software),
    software = recode(
      software,
      "Jamovi" = "jamovi"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(software),
    software != "",
    software != "NA",
    software != "Other (specify)",
    software %in% c(
      "SPSS",
      "Excel",

# --------------------------------------------------
# 3. PLOT STYLE
# --------------------------------------------------

main_col <- "#4657A9"

my_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15,
      colour = main_col,
      lineheight = .95
    ),

    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),

    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(
      colour = "grey88",
      linewidth = 0.35
    ),

    axis.text.x = element_text(
      size = 10.5,
      colour = "grey35"
    ),

    axis.text.y = element_text(
      size = 12,
      colour = "grey20",
      lineheight = .95
    ),

    plot.margin = margin(
      2, 8, 2, 2
    )
  )

# --------------------------------------------------
# 4. FUNCTION FOR STANDARD BAR PLOTS
# --------------------------------------------------

make_bar <- function(data, var, title) {

  data %>%
    filter(
      !is.na({{ var }}),
      {{ var }} != "Other"
    ) %>%
    count({{ var }}) %>%
    ggplot(
      aes(
        x = n,
        y = fct_rev({{ var }})
      )
    ) +
    geom_col(
      fill = main_col,
      alpha = 0.82
    ) +
    geom_text(
      aes(label = n),
      hjust = -0.18,
      size = 4.2,
      colour = "grey20"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(),
      expand = expansion(
        mult = c(0, .16)
      )
    ) +
    labs(title = title) +
    my_theme
}

# 5. INDIVIDUAL PLOTS

    )
```

## About the course

::: {.nonincremental}

20-hour (2 ECTS) Small Group Activity delivered in **blended format** <br> <br>

💻 **Part 1 online (10h)**

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}

`1.1.` `r fa("heart-pulse", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` `What happens in the body?` <br>
Stress responses and biosignals in user studies <br>

`1.2.` `r fa("microchip", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` `How can we measure it?`  <br>
Introduction to wearable tech <br><br>

:::

🏫 **Part 2 in person (10h)**

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}

`2.` `r fa("laptop-code", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` `Hands on wearables and biosignals` <br>
Practical activities & group project

:::

:::

## 💻 Part 1: theory, methods, & applications

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

1 live session + 9 online lectures with interactive activities on Moodle

:::

::: {.nonincremental}

`r fa("heart-pulse", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` `Stress responses and biosignals in user studies`

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

  1. The stress response and the autonomic nervous system
  2. Stress, cognitive appraisals, and recovery
  3. Biosignals and biomarkers of stress and recovery
  
:::
  
`r fa("microchip", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` `Introduction to wearable technologies`

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

  4. Wearable Technologies: Principles, Types and Applications
  5. ECG & PPG for measuring heart rate and HRV
  6. Electrodermal activity
  7. Accelerometry & actigraphy for measuring activity and sleep
  8. Can we trust wearable sensors? Validity, artefacts, ethics, and privacy

:::

:::

## 🏫 Part 2: hands-on activities & group project

::: {.nonincremental}

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

5 in-person sessions with practical activities + group project

1. `Wearable demos & project start` <br>
Case study, research questions, constructs, signals & sensors

2. `Study design & data recording` <br>
Hands-on data acquisition + group study protocol

3. `Signal pre-processing in` `r fa("r-project", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` <br>
Hands-on data pre-processing + group pre-processing plan

4. `From signals to user-study results in` `r fa("r-project", height = "1em", fill="#4657A9")` <br>
Data analysis and visualization + group analysis plan

5. `User Study Showcase` <br>
Group project presentations & peer feedback

:::

Participation in the in-person practical sessions is expected, as most of the group project <br>
and hands-on activities will be carried out during class. <br> You are free to use your own laptop or the computers available in the room.

## Target skills and knowledge

::: {.nonincremental}

<br>

::: {.column width="70%"}

1. `r fa("book", height = "1em",fill="#4657A9")` Understand the stress response and related cognitive constructs <br>

2. `r fa("microchip", height = "1em",fill="#4657A9")` Know and critically evaluate the main types of wearable sensors and associated biosignals <br>

3. `r fa("mobile-screen", height = "1em",fill="#4657A9")` Analyze and critically evaluate applications of wearable tech in user studies <br>

4. `r fa("compass-drafting", height = "1em",fill="#4657A9")` Design and implement user study protocols using wearable technologies <br>

5. `r fa("magnifying-glass-chart", height = "1em",fill="#4657A9")` Apply pre-processing, visualization, and analysis techniques to biosignals

:::

:::

## Evaluation and assessment criteria

::: {.nonincremental}
::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

There is no final exam. The course is assessed on a pass/fail basis based on the **assignments completed throughout the course**, including Moodle activities, hands-on data analysis exercises, and the **group project** developed during the practical sessions.

The group project will consist of designing a **wearable-based user study**, from the formulation of research questions to the definition of the user study, data pre-processing strategy, and analysis and visualization plan. The projects will be presented during the final meeting.

<br>

Across the course activities, students will be required to demonstrate their ability to:

- Design data acquisition protocols using wearable technologies
- Pre-process and analyze biosignals using R
- Critically interpret physiological and behavioural data
- Plan appropriate data analyses and visualizations
- Effectively communicate methodological choices and results

:::
:::

## Wearable tech & biosignals

<br>

Let's see some examples

LIVE🔴

## Wearable tech & biosignals *for user studies*

::: {.nonincremental}

A **wearable-based user study** uses body-worn sensors to collect physiological and behavioural data while people interact with technologies, systems, or other people through technology

::: {.column width="50%"}

- **User interaction**  

- **Psychological construct**  

- **Biosignal / behaviour** 

- **Interpretation in context**

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](img/wearable-VR.png){width="500px"}

:::

:::

The goal is not to “detect stress”, but to understand <br> how users respond to an interaction

## Two broad families of user studies

<br>

::: {.nonincremental}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}


### 👤📱<br>Human–Tech Interaction

The user interacts directly with a technological system:

- using a mobile app 
- navigation alert 
- interacting with a chatbot 
- working with a cobot 
- using a VR environment 

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### 👤📱👤<br>Tech-Mediated Interaction

Technology mediates interaction between people:

- remote collaboration 
- video calls 
- expert–novice interaction 
- online teamwork 
- *e*-learning 

:::
:::
:::

## What psychophysiological data can add

::: {.nonincremental}

They can help us study aspects of user experience that are difficult to capture with self-report and behavioral data alone:

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Arousal and activation
- Effort and workload
- Recovery after the interaction
- Task-related temporal dynamics
- Individual differences in <br>response patterns

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](img/user-stress.png){width="500px"}

:::

**But physiological data are meaningful only when interpreted together with task features, behaviour, and subjective experience**

:::

## Common misconceptions

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

> *A wearable can measure stress directly*

**No.** Wearables record biosignals, not psychological constructs

<br>

> *If heart rate increases, the user is stressed*

**Not necessarily.** Heart rate may increase because of movement,<br>posture, caffeine, or many other **confounding factors**

<br>

> *More biosignals and indices means better interpretation*

**Not necessarily.** Poorly contextualized biosignals can easily lead to<br>overinterpretation and cherry picking 🍒

:::

## From biosignals to interpretation

![](img/wearable-user.png){width="500px"}

::: {.nonincremental}

Wearable-based user studies requires a clear chain of reasoning:

- 👤 **What is the user doing?**

- 💡 **What construct are we interested in?**  

- ⚡ **Which biosignals could reflect relevant processes?**  

- ⌚ **Which sensor can measure it in this context?** 

- 💥 **What could confound the interpretation?**

:::
